name: HSV GTS-R (VS)
hook: Holden had no 5.7-litre V8, so its tuning arm made one by fitting the five-litre with a longer-throw crankshaft, then painted all 85 cars the same shouting yellow.
story:
Holden's V8 was five litres. That was the biggest it made. There was nothing larger in the parts bin.

So in the mid-1990s its performance partner, Holden Special Vehicles, built a bigger one. The trick was the crankshaft. Holden's own engine plant cast it. Harrop Engineering shared the machining, and gave it a longer throw. Same block, longer stroke. Five litres became 5.7. Pistons with shorter skirts came from ACL. Polished ports helped it breathe.

In the 1996 GTS-R, that engine made 215 kilowatts and 475 newton-metres. Still not enough? You could pay about ten thousand dollars more. Holden Racing Team engineers would strip your engine and blueprint it. That was worth another 10 to 15 kilowatts.

Then HSV painted every car the same colour. A loud yellow, called XU-3 Yellah. On the boot sat a carbon-fibre wing copied from the team's race cars.

It cost $75,000, the most expensive Holden yet. Only 85 were built. Seventy-five stayed in Australia. Ten crossed the Tasman to New Zealand.
description: The GTS-R was a limited-edition flagship built in 1996 by Holden Special Vehicles on the VS Commodore sedan. Its 5.7-litre pushrod V8 was HSV's own stroker, a Holden five-litre with a longer-stroke Harrop crankshaft. It drove the rear wheels through a Tremec T56 six-speed manual and a limited-slip differential. Every car was painted XU-3 Yellah and wore a carbon-fibre rear wing. At $75,000 it was the most expensive Holden of its day, and 85 were made.
